title: Probability
overview: Use tree diagrams and Venn diagrams to handle conditional probability and test for independence. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Use addition and multiplication rules in probability.
Distinguish mutually exclusive and independent events.
Model multi-stage situations with trees, Venn diagrams and combinations.

definitions.definition: Events that cannot occur together, so P(A∩B)=0.
Events where occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other.
P(A|B), the probability of A given B has occurred.
A′, the event that A does not occur.
The set of possible elementary outcomes.

sections.title: Addition and multiplication
content: For overlapping events, P(A∪B)=P(A)+P(B)−P(A∩B). Along successive branches multiply; across mutually exclusive complete routes add. Use complements for 'at least one'.

sections.title: Exclusive versus independent
content: Mutually exclusive non-zero events are not independent: if A occurs, B cannot. Test independence using P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B), or equivalently P(A|B)=P(A) when P(B)>0.
bullets: Do not infer independence from a diagram unless stated or shown.

sections.title: Conditional probability
content: Use P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B). The denominator is the condition—the reduced sample space. Tree diagrams encode this because second-stage probabilities sit on branches after the condition is known.
bullets: Read 'given that' before deciding the denominator.
Reverse conditionals P(A|B) and P(B|A) are generally different.

sections.title: Counting probability
content: When elementary outcomes are equally likely, probability=favourable/total. Use combinations for unordered selections and carefully account for colours, categories or restrictions in both numerator and denominator.
bullets: A Venn diagram can expose intersections and complements.
Check that final probabilities lie between 0 and 1.

examTips: Define events in words before using symbols.
Keep exact fractions through tree calculations where possible.
Show the mathematical setup and exact working before the final rounded answer; unsupported calculator output may not earn method marks.
commonMistakes: Using P(A) rather than P(B) as the denominator of P(A|B).
Keeping replacement probabilities unchanged in a without-replacement model.

quickRecall.question: Can two non-zero mutually exclusive events be independent?
quickRecall.answer: No; occurrence of one makes the other impossible.

quickRecall.question: What is the denominator of P(A|B)?
quickRecall.answer: P(B), because B is the restricted sample space.

quickRecall.question: How is 'at least one' often simplified?
What changes in a without-replacement tree?
quickRecall.answer: The second-stage totals and favourable counts depend on the first outcome.
